Scope creep for freelance developers: how to tell a bug from a change request (with a triage table)

2026-11-25

"It's a bug" is one of the most useful sentences in a client's vocabulary. Sometimes it really is a bug. Sometimes it means "the app doesn't do something I've just thought of", and the word "bug" quietly turns a new feature into free work.

Development projects grow in their own way. The requests sound small ("just add Google login", "it should work on my old tablet too", "can you load our customer list in?"), but each one can hide a day of work, a new third-party account, or a testing matrix that has doubled. And because a client can't see code, they can't see the difference between a one-line fix and a new feature either.

This article applies five common causes of scope creep to development work, follows a fictional project from sign-off to a month after launch, and gives you two things to keep: a "bug or change request?" triage table and exclusion lines for hosting, third-party APIs, the post-launch fix window and content entry.

Not legal advice. The wording below is for a plain-language scope summary or proposal that describes the work. It isn't a contract. Payment terms, IP ownership, liability, warranties and cancellation belong in a contract, ideally one reviewed by a qualified lawyer where you work.

Five causes of scope creep, in developer terms

Most scope creep on a dev project traces back to one of five gaps in what was agreed before the work started.

Cause How it shows up in dev work What to write down
Vague quantities "A simple dashboard" turns out to need four user roles, filters and CSV export Screens, user roles, integrations and reports, each listed by name
Unstated client tasks You assumed you'd get API keys, test data and the real content. The client assumed you'd sort all of it out What the client supplies, by when, and what happens if it's late
Hidden third parties A payment provider, an SMS service, the client's IT contractor or their hosting company sets the rules halfway through Each outside service, who owns the account, and what "integrate" covers
Unlimited feedback User testing never ends: every round of testing brings new "issues" that are really preferences How acceptance testing works, how long it lasts, and who signs off
No agreed change process Requests arrive in chat, in calls and in bug reports, and get done to keep things moving Where requests go, how they're sorted, and how they're priced

The fourth and fifth causes take a particular shape on software projects. A design revision looks like a revision. A change request often arrives dressed as a bug report, and it's sent through the channel you set up for bugs. That's why the triage table below matters.

Where development projects tend to stretch

Four areas come up again and again. Each needs one clear line in your scope summary.

Hosting and environments. Who pays for the server, who has the admin login, and who gets the call when it goes down at 2am? If the client owns the hosting account (so they keep control if you part ways), say so, and say what you'll set up there. Ongoing monitoring, backups and server updates are a service, not part of a build.

Third-party APIs. "Connect it to Stripe" or "send a text when the repair is ready" depends on a service you don't control. Name the service, the specific actions you'll build (for example "send one SMS when a job is marked ready"), and who creates and pays for the account. Then say what happens when the provider changes its API, prices or limits after handover: that's new work, not a fix.

Browser and device support. "It should work everywhere" can't be tested. List what you test on. Some front-end projects already define supported browsers in a Browserslist config. Its defaults query is documented as > 0.5%, last 2 versions, Firefox ESR, not dead (Browserslist README). That's fine for your build tools, but a client won't know what it means. In the scope summary, describe what you'll actually test on, in plain words: "current versions of Chrome, Safari, Firefox and Edge, on desktop and on phone-sized screens". If the client's front desk runs an old machine, find out now and decide whether to add it.

Content and data entry. Code that displays 300 products doesn't put the 300 products in. Say who enters content, who cleans up an existing spreadsheet before import, and how many records or pages you'll load yourself, if any.

The free piece: "bug or change request?" triage

When something is reported, run it through four questions in order. Stop at the first one that gives you an answer.

  1. Was this behaviour described in the agreed scope (feature list, acceptance notes or the screens you signed off)? If not, it's a change request, however it was labelled.
  2. Does it happen in a supported browser, device or environment? If not, it's a request to extend support.
  3. Is the cause in your code? If it's caused by a third-party service, the hosting, a plugin someone else installed, or content and data entered by the client, it isn't a defect in your work. Diagnosing it may still take time, so agree how that time is handled.
  4. Is it inside the fix window? If yes, fix it at no extra cost. If not, quote it or handle it under a support plan.

Here's how that plays out on common reports:

What the client says Likely verdict Why
"The signup form errors when an email has a + in it" Bug Signup was in scope, and a valid email address should work
"Login should work with Google too" Change request (new feature) Google login was never in the feature list
"The layout breaks on my 2016 tablet" Change request (extended support), unless that device is listed Testing covered the agreed list only
"Texts stopped sending on Tuesday" Check the third party first A provider outage, expired billing or an API change could be the cause; fix it free if your code is at fault
"The prices on the menu page are wrong" Content issue The client entered the prices; you can fix them as a favour or under a support plan
"It's slow now that we have 20,000 records" Clarify Depends on whether the scope said how much data the app should handle
"Can the Save button be green?" Change request (or a revision, if a design round is still open) It works as agreed. This is a preference

The verdicts are a starting point for a conversation, not a ruling. If a report is genuinely ambiguous, a small goodwill fix is often worth more than the argument.

Fictional worked example: a repair tracker for a bike shop

Fictional example. The developer, the client and every request below are invented to show the method. There are no prices in this example on purpose: use your own.

The project. Tomas is a freelance developer. A two-person bike repair shop wants "a simple web app to track repairs and text customers when their bike's ready". After the intake call he writes a scope summary. These lines matter later:

  • Screens: job list, job detail, new job form, customer list. Two user roles: owner and mechanic.
  • SMS: one text per job, sent when a job is marked "ready", via [SMS PROVIDER]. You create and pay for the account and share the API key by [DATE].
  • Hosting: on your [HOSTING] account. I set up the app and the database. Backups, monitoring and server updates after launch aren't included.
  • Testing: current Chrome and Safari on desktop, plus iPhone and Android phone-sized screens.
  • Data: I import your existing customer spreadsheet once, if you send it as a CSV with one customer per row. Clean-up of that spreadsheet isn't included.
  • Acceptance: one week of testing by you after the staging release. Issues are sent in one list. Launch follows your "accepted" email.
  • Fix window: 30 days after launch for anything that doesn't work as described here. New features and changes are quoted first.

The shop owner replies to confirm. In the table below, out-of-scope requests are labelled with one of the four types from the out-of-scope request email guide (tiny favour, new deliverable, extra revision round, changed goal), so each one has a ready-made reply.

When Request Type What the scope line made easy
Week 2 SMS account isn't set up by the agreed date Not a request: a late dependency Tomas builds the rest and points to the SMS line; the texting step waits for the key
Week 3 Customer spreadsheet arrives with names and phone numbers in one column Not a request: a data question The data line says clean-up isn't included; Tomas offers to quote it or send a sample row to copy
Week 4 (testing) "Can the job list show the oldest jobs first?" Tiny favour A one-line sort change. Tomas does it, says so, and logs it
Week 4 (testing) "Mechanics should be able to log the parts they use, with stock levels" New deliverable Not on the screen list. Tomas quotes it as phase two
2 weeks after launch "The ready text sends twice sometimes" Bug (in window) Described in scope, happens in normal use, cause is in the code. Fixed at no charge
5 weeks after launch "It's a bug: customers can't book a repair slot online" New deliverable, reported as a bug Online booking was never in scope, and the fix window has ended anyway

The last request is the one that needs care. The owner isn't trying to get free work. From the front of the shop, "customers can't book online" feels like something broken. Here's the reply Tomas sends, and it works as a template for any change that arrives as a bug report.

Reply script: when a "bug" is a change request

Hi [NAME],

Thanks for flagging this. I've checked it against the scope we
agreed on [DATE]: the app is working as described there, and online
booking wasn't part of the build. So this isn't a fault, but it's
a sensible next step and I can see why customers are asking.

Two ways forward:

- Quote it: I'll send a short quote for online booking by [DAY],
  including what it would need from you (for example, which time
  slots customers can choose).
- Note it for later: I'll add it to the phase-two list and we can
  look at it together with [OTHER PENDING REQUEST].

Separately, if you spot anything that doesn't work the way the
scope describes, send it over and I'll look at it as a fix.

Best,
[YOUR NAME]

The script does three things: it names the document instead of the person, gives two options, and keeps the door open for real bugs so the client keeps reporting them.

Copy-paste: exclusion and boundary lines for dev projects

Adapt these and delete any that don't apply. The out-of-scope section examples have a wider development list and tips on keeping exclusions friendly. Not legal advice and not a contract: these lines sit alongside your contract and should match it.

HOSTING: The app runs on your [PROVIDER] account, which you own and
pay for. I set up [app / database / domain connection] there. After
launch, server updates, backups and uptime monitoring aren't
included unless we agree a support plan.

THIRD-PARTY SERVICES: The build connects to [SERVICE] for [specific
actions]. You create, own and pay for the account and send me the
keys by [DATE]. If the provider changes its API, pricing or limits
after launch, updating the app is quoted as new work.

SUPPORTED BROWSERS AND DEVICES: [Current versions of ...] on
[desktop / phone / tablet] screen sizes. Other browsers, devices or
older versions are quoted if needed.

FIX WINDOW: For [30] days after launch I fix, at no extra cost,
anything that doesn't work as described in this summary. New
features, changed behaviour and design preferences are change
requests, quoted before I start.

CONTENT AND DATA: You enter [products / pages / users] through the
admin screens. I import [one file / up to N records] in [format].
Cleaning or reformatting existing data isn't included.

ACCEPTANCE: You test the staging version for [5] working days and
send one list of issues. Launch follows your "accepted" email.
Requests after acceptance follow the change process below.

CHANGES: Send new requests by [email / the shared tracker], not
chat. I'll reply within [2] working days with whether it's a fix,
a quick favour, or something to quote.

Where this fits

Write these lines before you put a price on the project, so the quote and the boundaries describe the same job:

  1. Ask your intake questions, including which outside services, accounts and data the project depends on.
  2. Write the scope summary with the lines above, and get the client to confirm it in writing.
  3. During the project, run every report through the triage questions and answer with options.

If you also build marketing sites, the web designer version of this map covers pages, content deadlines and design approval.

The limits

  • Triage won't settle every case. Some reports sit in a grey area, and a quick goodwill fix can be the right call. Log it either way, so a pattern is visible.
  • Gaps will still turn up. When a report falls between your lines, agree how to treat it with the client now, then add a line to your template for next time.
  • It isn't a contract. Liability for defects, warranties and payment disputes are contract territory.
